intuition: A single straight diagonal leg sailed across the wind when zigzagging upwind toward a destination you cannot reach directly.
practicalTip: Hold the boat in close-hauled (bolina) on one bordo until you reach the layline, then tack onto the opposite bordo.

commonPhrases.context: Crew alert before a tack or gybe
Calling right-of-way when crossing other boats

relatedConcepts.relationship: Tacking back and forth along multiple legs
Turn executed to switch to the opposite leg
Close-hauled point of sail held along the leg

intuition: Zigzagging back and forth across the wind in alternating diagonal legs to travel towards an upwind destination.
practicalTip: Keep the boat close to the edge of the wind on each leg to minimize the total distance sailed.

commonPhrases.phrase: Dobbiamo bordeggiare per entrare nel canale.
commonPhrases.meaning: We need to tack back and forth to enter the channel.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Each individual diagonal leg of the zigzag
The tacking turn executed between legs
No-go wind sector you cannot sail straight into

intuition: The sideways slide of a boat pushed by the wind, despite the keel and daggerboard resisting lateral motion in the water.
practicalTip: Aim slightly upwind of your target buoy or harbour entrance to compensate for the sideways drift.

commonPhrases.context: Warning when navigating close to shallow water or rocks

commonPhrases.phrase: C'è molto scarroccio con questo vento.
commonPhrases.meaning: There's heavy leeway with this wind.
commonPhrases.context: Helmsman noticing drift on the compass course

relatedConcepts.relationship: Underwater foil countering this sideways drift
Course steered vs actual track made good
Point of sail where leeway is most pronounced

intuition: Adjusting the angle of a sail relative to the wind so air flows smoothly across both surfaces like an airplane wing.
practicalTip: Ease the sheet until the forward edge begins to flutter (fileggiare), then trim in just enough to smooth it out.

commonPhrases.meaning: Trim the mainsail to the wind!
Sail is trimmed and drawing properly!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Hauling in sheet to flatten and trim sail
Easing out sheet until smooth flow reattaches
Flutter warning that the sail is under-trimmed

intuition: Pulling in a control line or sheet to bring the sail closer to the center of the boat, flattening it for sailing upwind.
practicalTip: Pull smoothly hand-over-hand while keeping your fingers clear of the winch drum.

commonPhrases.meaning: Sheet in as tight as possible / hauled flat!

commonPhrases.context: Trimmer command after completing a tack

relatedConcepts.relationship: Easing line out
The control line being hauled in
Trim goal achieved by adjusting sheet tension

intuition: Easing or letting out a sheet or line to open up the sail angle as the boat turns away from the wind.
practicalTip: Never let go of the line abruptly unless emergency depowering is needed; let it slip controlled under tension.

commonPhrases.context: Emergency depower during a heavy knockdown gust

commonPhrases.meaning: Ease a little bit of sheet!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Hauling line in
Flutter warning if line is eased too far
The control line being eased out

intuition: The flapping or fluttering of a sail when it is angled too far into the wind or when the sheet is eased too far.
practicalTip: A flapping sail generates drag and noise instead of forward lift; trim the sheet in or bear away until it stops.

commonPhrases.meaning: The sail is luffing, sheet in!
Let it luff to slow down!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Aerodynamic trim state that stops flutter
Action required to trim in and stop flutter
Sails flutter completely when pointed in dead zone

intuition: The wind you actually feel on the moving boat. It combines the real natural wind with the headwind created by the boat's forward speed.
practicalTip: Always trim sails and read the wind pennant (mostravento) based on apparent wind, not true wind.

commonPhrases.phrase: Guarda il vento apparente sul mostravento!
commonPhrases.meaning: Check the apparent wind on the masthead vane!
commonPhrases.context: Skipper coaching helmsman on wind angle

commonPhrases.phrase: Più corriamo veloci, più il vento gira in prua.
commonPhrases.meaning: The faster we sail, the more the wind shifts forward.

relatedConcepts.relationship: True atmospheric wind measured at rest
Masthead indicator showing apparent wind angle
Point of sail where apparent wind is strongest

intuition: The true direction and speed of the meteorological wind across the water, independent of the boat's movement.
practicalTip: Look at flags on shore or ripples on the water before leaving port to judge true wind direction.

commonPhrases.phrase: Il vento reale viene da nord.
commonPhrases.meaning: The true wind is coming from the north.

relatedConcepts.relationship: What moving boat sails actually experience
Compass rose tracking true wind directions

intuition: Turning the bow (front) of the boat through the eye of the wind to switch which side the wind hits the sails.
practicalTip: Carry good boat speed before turning so momentum pushes the boat through the dead zone.

commonPhrases.context: Skipper call alerting crew before putting helm over

commonPhrases.phrase: Molla la scotta vecchia, passa la nuova!
commonPhrases.meaning: Release old sheet, take up new sheet!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Bow crosses wind vs stern
The no-go sector crossed during the turn
Switches the boat to the opposite leg
The bow turned through the eye of the wind

intuition: To turn the bow of the boat through the wind to change tack from port to starboard or vice versa.
practicalTip: Push the tiller smoothly and avoid slamming the rudder hard over, which acts as a brake.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Turning through stern
Tiller pushed toward sail to initiate turn
Changing legs across the wind
Bringing the bow through the wind

intuition: Turning the stern (back) of the boat through the wind when sailing downwind, causing the boom to swing across rapidly.
practicalTip: Center the boom with the mainsheet before turning through the wind to prevent an uncontrolled violent swing.

commonPhrases.meaning: Watch your heads for the boom!
commonPhrases.context: Warning crew as the boom swings across the cockpit

relatedConcepts.relationship: Stern crosses wind vs bow
Dead downwind run preceding the gybe
Heavy spar swinging rapidly across cockpit
The stern turned through the eye of the wind

intuition: To turn the stern of the boat through the wind while sailing off the wind, shifting the boom to the opposite side.
practicalTip: Coordinate sheet trimming and helm smoothly so the boom travels across under control.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Turning through bow
Controlling boom during rapid crossing
Dead downwind course required before turn
Bringing the stern through the wind

intuition: Steering the boat closer toward the direction the wind is coming from, tightening your angle to the wind.
practicalTip: Push the tiller away from you (toward the wind/sail) to head up and depower during a strong gust.

commonPhrases.context: Depowering the sails to keep the boat flat

relatedConcepts.relationship: Heading up vs bearing away
Tiller pushed away from body toward sail
Sails luff if you head up too far
Heeling increases as boat heads closer to wind

intuition: The action or command to turn closer into the wind.
practicalTip: Keep an eye on the telltales on the jib to avoid turning too far into the dead zone.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Bear away from wind
Tiller direction pointing bow into wind
Steering higher toward close-hauled limit

intuition: Steering the boat away from the direction the wind is coming from, turning further downwind.
practicalTip: Pull the tiller toward you (away from wind) to bear away, and remember to ease the sheets as you turn.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Bearing away vs heading up
Tiller pulled toward body away from sail
Required sheet easing as boat bears away

intuition: The action or command to turn away from the wind.
practicalTip: Easing the sails allows the boat to accelerate as you bear away.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Head up into wind
Coordinated trimmer action when bearing away

intuition: A self-balancing 'parking' maneuver where the jib is sheeted to the wrong side (backed) and the helm is turned into wind, bringing the boat to a stable, gentle drift.
practicalTip: Use this maneuver in heavy weather or whenever the crew needs a safe break to reef sails, eat lunch, or attend to repairs.

commonPhrases.context: Deciding to pause the boat in open water

commonPhrases.phrase: Lega la barra e lascia il fiocco a collo!
commonPhrases.meaning: Lash the helm and leave the jib backed!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Heavy weather storm variant on cruising yachts
Backwinded jib held against rudder to stall boat
Setup maneuver — tacking without easing jib

intuition: Heaving-to in heavy weather; setting sails and helm to ride out high winds and rough seas with minimal drift and stress on the vessel.
practicalTip: Once balanced in cappa, the boat creates a smooth slick of disturbed water (scia) to windward that breaks oncoming waves.

commonPhrases.phrase: Siamo alla cappa, la barca è tranquilla.
commonPhrases.meaning: We are hove-to, the boat is riding smoothly.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Dinghy counterpart for resting in calm waters
Reefing down mainsail before locking helm
Gentle controlled downwind drift while ahull

intuition: The leaning or tilting of the boat to one side caused by the force of the wind pushing sideways against the sails.
practicalTip: Hiking out (cinghie puntapiedi) with your body weight counters heeling, keeping the daggerboard vertical and efficient.

commonPhrases.meaning: Too much heel, spill some wind!
commonPhrases.context: Reducing heel for better boat control

commonPhrases.meaning: Everyone hike out on the toe-straps!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Crew hiking out on straps
Foil leverage countering boat heeling torque
Hiking straps securing feet to cockpit floor

intuition: To heel or lean over to one side under wind pressure on the sails.
practicalTip: A small amount of heel is normal, but excessive heeling causes the rudder to drag and the boat to slide sideways.

commonPhrases.phrase: La barca sbanda troppo, lasca la randa!
commonPhrases.meaning: The boat is heeling too much, ease the mainsail!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Quick helm reaction to spill excess wind
The physical heel angle produced by wind
Hardware enabling crew to lean outboard

intuition: The ~90° cone pointing directly into the wind where sails cannot generate aerodynamic lift and will only flutter uselessly.
practicalTip: Never try to point directly at an upwind mark inside this angle; sail at roughly 45° to the wind on a close-hauled course.

commonPhrases.meaning: You're in the dead zone, bear away!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Closest sailable angle bordering this sector
Quick turn required to pass through dead zone
Sails flap helplessly if pointed inside

intuition: The point of sail closest to the wind (roughly 45° off the wind direction), where the sails act as wings generating forward lift.
practicalTip: Keep the sails sheeted in tight and watch the telltales (filetti) to steer right on the wind's edge.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Forbidden upwind boundary limit (~45°)
Next point of sail downwind (90° beam reach)
Maximum sheet trim hauled flat for upwind
Side leeway drift is strongest at this angle

intuition: The point of sail where the wind blows directly perpendicular (90°) onto the side of the boat; typically the fastest and easiest point of sail.
practicalTip: Set the sails halfway out so the boom points roughly toward the leeward corner of the transom.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Upwind neighbor (45° close-hauled beat)
Downwind neighbor (135° broad reach)
Fastest point of sail directly across wind (90°)

intuition: A broad reach point of sail where the wind comes over the rear quarter of the boat (roughly 120°–140° off the bow).
practicalTip: Ease the boom out broad and raise the daggerboard halfway to reduce drag when sailing on a broad reach.

commonPhrases.meaning: Bear away to a broad reach!
commonPhrases.context: Course change after rounding the windward mark

relatedConcepts.relationship: Upwind neighbor — 90° beam reach
Downwind neighbor — 180° dead run
Beating hard upwind

intuition: Sailing dead downwind (180° off the wind), with the wind pushing the boat directly from behind.
practicalTip: Beware of unintentional accidental gybes (strambata involontaria); keep a boom preventer rigged or watch the wind vane closely.

commonPhrases.phrase: Attenti all'abbattuta in fil di ruota!
commonPhrases.meaning: Watch out for an accidental gybe running dead downwind!

commonPhrases.context: Jib to one side, main to the other

relatedConcepts.relationship: Upwind neighbor — broad reach with clean flow
Accidental gybe danger on this 180° run
Boom extended fully outboard across boat

intuition: Dropping or letting go of the anchor into the sea bed to secure the vessel at rest.
practicalTip: Stop the boat's forward momentum completely and begin drifting backwards slowly before dropping anchor.

commonPhrases.meaning: The anchor has dug in / set!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Ground tackle dropped to sea bed
Chain & rode scope paid out relative to depth
Boat momentum that must be killed before drop

intuition: Securing a line firmly to a cleat (galloccia) or bitt by wrapping it with an initial turn and figure-eight locking hitches.
practicalTip: Do not add too many locking hitches on a cleat; one clean figure-eight with a half-hitch is secure and will never jam.

commonPhrases.context: Securing a halyard or mooring line
Preparing to untie or lower sail

relatedConcepts.relationship: Cleat where figure-eight turn is secured
Dock bollard for securing heavy mooring lines
Coiling excess line after securing turn

intuition: Coiling a line neatly into loops so it stows without tangling and is ready to run free instantly when needed.
practicalTip: Roll a clockwise twist with your thumb and forefinger on each loop to prevent kinks and hockles.

commonPhrases.meaning: Line coiled and clear to run.

relatedConcepts.relationship: Active sheet coiled neatly to prevent foul-ups
Tying off line before coiling tail
Halyard tail coiled and hung on mast pin

intuition: The forward momentum and coasting glide that a boat retains through the water after propulsion has stopped.
practicalTip: Judge your remaining abbrivo carefully when approaching a dock or mooring buoy so you stop right at the destination.

commonPhrases.meaning: We still have too much way on / forward momentum!

commonPhrases.context: Stalling during a tack or maneuver

relatedConcepts.relationship: Headway killed before dropping anchor
Inertia carrying boat through dead zone during tack
Residual glide used to ease smoothly into dock

intuition: A capsize where a dinghy is knocked over on its side into the water by a heavy gust or crew balance error.
practicalTip: Never stay under the overturned sail; immediately swim around to the daggerboard and apply downward foot pressure.

commonPhrases.meaning: Climb onto the daggerboard to right the boat!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Recovery — standing on centerboard to right hull
Exterior foil crew climbs onto for leverage
Extreme heel angle that trips the capsize

intuition: Righting an overturned dinghy back upright by standing on the daggerboard and using body leverage against the hull.
practicalTip: Check that the mainsheet is eased free so the boat doesn't instantly sail away or capsize again as it pops upright.

commonPhrases.meaning: Put your weight on the tip of the daggerboard!

relatedConcepts.relationship: The capsize emergency this maneuver recovers
The daggerboard used as a righting lever
Hiking straps enabling crew to counter heel

intuition: The retractable underwater foil (daggerboard/centerboard) that counters the sideways push of the wind and converts it into forward motion.
practicalTip: Fully down for close-hauled upwind sailing (bolina); pull up halfway or more when running downwind to reduce hydrodynamic drag.

commonPhrases.phrase: Giù tutta la deriva per la bolina!
commonPhrases.meaning: All the way down with the daggerboard for upwind!

commonPhrases.phrase: Alza la deriva a metà al lasco!
commonPhrases.meaning: Raise the daggerboard halfway on a reach!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Sideways leeway drift resisted by this foil
Trunk housing inside hull where board retracts
Fixed keel on yachts vs mobile board
Point of sail requiring board fully down

intuition: The forward-most part of the hull (the bow), designed to slice through waves and establish the boat's heading.
practicalTip: Watch the bow during maneuvers: in a tack (virata) the prua crosses through the eye of the wind; in irons (angolo morto), the prua stops dead.

commonPhrases.meaning: Head to wind / Bow into the wind!
commonPhrases.context: Command to bring the boat directly into the eye of the wind to hoist sails or stop
Describing wind direction coming from dead ahead

relatedConcepts.relationship: The stern at the aft of the vessel
Maneuver where the prua crosses through the eye of the wind
The no-go sector where wind blows directly onto the prua

intuition: The aft-most section of the hull (the stern), which houses the rudder (timone), transom (specchio di poppa), and cockpit.
practicalTip: When sailing downwind with the wind over the poppa (fil di ruota), watch the mainsail carefully to prevent an accidental, violent gybe (strambata).

commonPhrases.meaning: Fair winds / Wind from behind! (Traditional wish for good fortune)
commonPhrases.context: Sailing downwind with tailwind; also used colloquially as good luck

commonPhrases.meaning: Pass the stern through the wind!

relatedConcepts.relationship: The bow at the front of the vessel
Maneuver where the poppa crosses through the eye of the wind
Point of sail running directly before the wind over the poppa

intuition: The right-hand side of a boat when facing forward toward the bow (starboard). Crucial for maritime rules of the road.
practicalTip: When on a starboard tack (mura a dritta — wind blowing onto your starboard side), you have right-of-way over boats on port tack.

commonPhrases.context: Helm command to alter course to the right

commonPhrases.meaning: Starboard boat has right of way!

relatedConcepts.relationship: Port / left-hand side looking forward
Forward orientation reference when determining dritta

intuition: The left-hand side of a boat when facing forward toward the bow (port). Marked by red navigation lights at night.
practicalTip: A boat on port tack (mura a sinistra) must yield and give way to any boat sailing on starboard tack.

commonPhrases.context: Helm command to adjust course to the left

commonPhrases.phrase: Mura a sinistra, dobbiamo dare precedenza!
commonPhrases.meaning: Port tack, we must give way!
commonPhrases.context: Tactical rule reminder when crossing other boats

relatedConcepts.relationship: Starboard / right-hand side looking forward
Forward orientation reference when determining sinistra
